meta.title: Shut Out
meta.dek: Trump banned three news organizations from the White House. Six days later a judge he appointed ordered them back in. The claims, the record, and what comes next.
meta.status: Passes restored under a 14-day court order
meta.statusText: A federal judge ordered the hard passes restored on September 24, and journalists from all three outlets were back inside the White House that day. That evening CNN and MS NOW reporters were kept out of Xi's state-dinner arrival, an event the order does not clearly cover. The network pool, idle since September 21, resumed on September 25. The order is temporary: it runs fourteen days. The outlets' motion for a longer one is due September 28, and the court has said it "intends to rule expeditiously."

deck: On September 18, 2026, the president posted that, "effective immediately," he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The next morning the Secret Service took their reporters' badges at the gate. He named no story. His lawyers later cited national security. A federal judge he appointed found nothing in the record to support that, and ordered the badges returned.

Below: the six days in order, what the government claimed set against what the record shows, who objected and who defended it, the precedent the case turns on, and what happens next. Every fact is sourced. Every opinion is labeled.

events.title: Trump announces the ban on Truth Social
body: He posted that, "effective immediately," he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" He added: "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow."
He named no story. CNN reported that he did not "identify any specific reporting that prompted his social media declaration."

events.title: In the Oval Office: 'a very simple ban'
body: Asked what the ban would look like, he said, per the Roll Call Factbase transcript: "Oh, the ban on the free press, right? Uh, a very simple ban. I don't want them in my office. I don't want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can."

Asked how it squared with his oath: "Uh, because they're fake news. Uh, you get so tired of reading and seeing fake news." Asked what set it off: "it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it." He said the ban could be lifted if the outlets "could straighten themselves out."

events.title: The correspondents’ association objects, led by a Fox News reporter
body: The White House Correspondents' Association, whose president, Jacqui Heinrich, is Fox News's senior White House correspondent, said: "The WHCA stands in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MSNOW, and POLITICO who are being singled out for doing their jobs."

Ari Fleischer, George W. Bush's press secretary, wrote that he agreed several outlets were biased and unfair, and then rejected the remedy: "Banning them from the WH is not the solution... Don't ban them. Or one day they'll ban us."

events.title: The Secret Service takes the badges at the gate
body: Hard passes were deactivated and physically confiscated at the security kiosk. MS NOW's Akayla Gardner: "officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled. I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

"I asked him if he could provide an explanation as to why it had been deactivated," CNN's Betsy Klein said. "He said he had no further information." Politico's Cheyenne Haslett had her pass taken as well. None of them received written notice or a reason.

body: Sen. John Barrasso, asked on NBC whether the ban violated the Constitution: "No. I believe the press has an obligation to report fairly." House Majority Leader Steve Scalise told ABC: "Well, I don't know why he did it. I don't know what the background is."

events.title: The White House pulls CNN from the television pool
body: The daily guidance removed CNN from the next day's schedule. CNN had been the assigned pool network for Monday and Tuesday, including Trump's address to the U.N. General Assembly. Pool footage goes to the other networks and to "the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN."

events.title: A new reason appears: national security
body: Trump posted: "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS... It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!" CNBC noted that he had not cited national security before.

events.title: The networks refuse to replace CNN
body: Fox News's Washington bureau chief, Bryan Boughton, who chairs the television pool, told subscribers that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President," and that "There will be no replacement pool put in place."

Fox News, ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC said jointly: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting."

events.title: The outlets sue
body: Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump was filed in federal court in Washington, pleading Fifth Amendment due process, First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The complaint opens: "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles."

It was assigned to Judge Timothy J. Kelly, whom Trump appointed in 2017. In 2018 Kelly heard CNN's suit over Jim Acosta's revoked pass and, as ABC reported, "ruled in Acosta's favor after finding that the Trump White House did not afford him proper due process."

events.title: Before any ruling, Trump promises an appeal
body: He posted that the judge "was, sadly, appointed by 'TRUMP.' In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we'll go for appeal."

The White House published a defense titled "White House Access Is a Privilege, Not a Right," which says: "The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool."

body: The Washington Post said it would "not publish any photographs of today's presidential events... until midnight Eastern Time," and Mediaite reported that the New York Times, the Associated Press, Reuters, Getty Images and AFP joined. NPR, a member of the White House radio pool, declined to broadcast audio of Trump.

events.title: The White House launches its own channel
body: It launched "Trump TV," a 24-hour stream of past official clips on the White House's YouTube channel and app. NOTUS reported that its first livestream was a two-month-old clip of the president at Mount Rushmore.

events.title: At the U.N., Trump tells CNN it should not be there
body: Covering him on U.N. credentials, CNN's Kaitlan Collins was told: "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me." Collins said on air that CNN had never said that.
Asked whether he would let the outlets back in if he lost in court, he said the judge would probably rule against him, and: "I think we have a right to clean out fake news."

body: "We're not closing CNN," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on NBC. "There aren't a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it's called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They're just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House."

events.title: The Justice Department asks the court to discard the precedent
body: The government's opposition opens: "After all, access to the White House is a privilege—not a right." On the 1977 case that governs press credentials it does not argue compliance. It argues "that decision is wrong and should be overruled," and says the same of the 2020 appeals-court decision that built on it.
It adds: "At the very least, no injunction may run against the President."

events.title: Four days after the ban, the letters
body: The White House emailed each outlet a letter dated that day, one day after the lawsuit. CNN's arrived at 10:30 p.m. Each says: "This letter is to provide notice that the President has made the determination to revoke hard passes for members of your organization," and sets a deadline: "please submit a written response to us in writing via email by 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, 2026."

No individual signed them. They close "White House Press Office," and they are addressed to the organizations, not to the reporters whose passes were taken. The government's brief calls this "sufficient post-deprivation process."

events.title: Trump calls the judge 'totally disloyal'
body: He posted that the outlets are "sick, treasonous, and demented" and that they have "a great, for them, and totally disloyal Judge." Judge Kelly is a Trump appointee.

sources.text: Trump's Truth (Defending Democracy Together archive of Truth Social posts): post of September 22, 2026, 11:53 p.m.

events.title: Fifty-one news organizations file against the White House
body: The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents' Association and 49 news organizations asked the court to restore access. Fox News Network is among them. The brief calls the stated reasons "transparently viewpoint discriminatory" and says "unassailable First Amendment law makes any viewpoint-based decision to bar reporters from a nonpublic forum constitutionally repugnant."

sources.text: Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump: Brief of Amici Curiae Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, White House Correspondents' Association and 49 Media Organizations, ECF 18-1 (September 23, 2026)

events.title: The hearing: 'I have to apply them'
body: Judge Kelly told the government he is bound by the cases it wanted discarded: "Maybe they were, maybe they weren't, but currently as a district judge I have to apply them." On the record before him, due process "wasn't followed here." On the letters: "I don't know [that] a letter they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of standards that they'd have to conform their conduct to."
He did not rule from the bench, and said he would decide "as soon as I can."

events.title: Two of the accusations come apart
body: The Associated Press reported that an anonymous-source story cited against Politico "appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House itself." The Washington Post, which reviewed a recording of the call, reported: "The Associated Press, Bloomberg and CNBC were among several outlets who reported on the call, citing a senior administration official, but were not banned from the White House."

MS NOW's Washington bureau chief swore that of the three MS NOW articles the letter cites, only one was written by a journalist who held a White House hard pass, and that pass was renewed a week after the story now cited against the network.

events.title: The order: 'full stop'
body: Judge Kelly granted the temporary restraining order and directed that the passes be restored immediately. To the argument that Sherrill and Karem were wrongly decided, the order answers: "Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop."

He found the government's only standard "is so vague it hardly does the trick," and that "[N]othing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns." The order runs fourteen days, binds the defendants "except for President Trump," and was not stayed.

events.title: Turned away at the gate anyway
body: Journalists from all three outlets were refused entry. Betsy Klein was denied at 9 a.m., and her request to have her pass back was refused. The outlets filed an emergency notice: "Defendants have already repeatedly violated the Court's Order," adding that the government's lawyers had not responded to a request to call the judge together.

sources.text: Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump: Corrected Notice of Defendants' Non-Compliance with Temporary Restraining Order and Request for Immediate Hearing, ECF 26 (September 24, 2026)

events.title: The passes come back
body: Kelly ordered the government to answer by 12:30 p.m. The White House's press operations director, Micah Stopperich, filed a sworn timeline: her team was told shortly after 7 a.m. to turn the badges back on, and the Secret Service indicated shortly after 9 a.m. that the passes were "back on." CNN and MS NOW journalists were admitted at noon. Politico said its access came that afternoon.

The judge accepted the explanation and declined to hold an emergency hearing. He set the next stage, with a motion for a preliminary injunction due September 28, and said the court "intends to rule expeditiously."

events.title: In the Oval Office with Xi, photographers only
body: The meeting with Xi Jinping had been scheduled as closed press. At the last minute the White House admitted still photographers only and "denied requests from the rest of the pool, including reporters who would be asking questions, to join." In front of the photographers, Trump remarked that Xi has the friendliest press corps in the world. The Associated Press added: "China is one of the most oppressive environments for journalists in the world."

sources.text: Associated Press via Bangor Daily News: The Latest: Trump hails 'truly great friendship' with China's Xi Jinping as summit begins (September 24, 2026)
CNN: Live updates: Trump hosts Xi for US-China summit in Washington, DC (September 24, 2026)

events.title: 'They refused to be there'
body: Trump posted that CNN and "MSDNC" "refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years," Xi's morning arrival. CNN called the claim false. Xi arrived at about 10 a.m.; CNN's Betsy Klein was not let back onto the grounds until around noon, and both networks covered the arrival on their digital platforms. The television pool, CNN included, did not film it because the networks were still waiting for the White House to confirm that CNN could take its turn.

events.title: Kept out of the state dinner arrival
body: Xi's evening arrival was open to pre-credentialed media, a wider group than the pool. About an hour before he was due, CNN reported, the White House said it could cover the arrival with a photojournalist and an audio technician only, while other networks were permitted reporters and producers. MS NOW's Laura Barrón-López said she was told she could not be let in.

The White House's rapid-response account wrote, "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call." The restraining order restored the hard passes; whether it reaches event credentials is unsettled, and Deadline noted that the evening exclusion "does not appear to be addressed in Kelly's order."

events.title: The pool comes back
body: The network television pool, paused since September 21, resumed. CBS had the White House duty and CNN the in-town pool at the National Archives, where the networks carried its feed of Trump and Xi. CNN anchor Pamela Brown: "CNN's access to the White House has been restored, and the TV pool appears to be functioning as normal." The outlets' lawyer, Ted Boutrous, said they believe pool access "is covered by the temporary restraining order."

events.title: 'It's been very fair'
body: At a tea meeting with Xi and the two first ladies, Trump said, "And we appreciate the fair coverage. It's been very fair."

claims.claim: After all, access to the White House is a privilege—not a right.
claims.found: Two appeals-court decisions say a reporter’s pass is protected, and a district judge is bound by them.
claims.detail: Sherrill v. Knight (1977) treats a correspondent’s interest in a White House pass as a liberty interest that cannot be denied without due process, and Karem v. Trump (2020) holds that a pass already issued cannot be suspended without it. The government asked the court to treat both as wrongly decided. The judge: "Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop."

claims.claim: trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information
claims.who: White House letters to the three outlets, September 22
claims.found: Nothing that predates the lawsuit points to national security as the motive.
claims.detail: Trump’s announcement cited "FAKE NEWS," and asked what set it off he said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years." He first invoked national security on September 21, the morning the outlets announced their suit, and CNBC noted he had not cited it before. The order: "[N]othing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns."

watch.text: The letters gave each outlet until 5 p.m. to respond by email. The record does not say what the White House will do with the responses, or whether that process continues now that the passes are back under court order.

watch.title: The fourteen days run out
watch.text: The restraining order runs fourteen days from September 24. The briefing schedule is set inside that window.

watch.title: Events and the pool
watch.text: The order restored the hard passes. The outlets' lawyer says it also covers pool access; after the state-dinner exclusion, the White House said they do not get "free rein" to every event.

watch.title: An appeal
watch.text: Trump promised an appeal on September 21, before there was a ruling to appeal. The judge noted that restraining orders are generally unappealable.

watch.title: "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow"
watch.text: On the day of the ban Trump also called the New York Times and the Washington Post "fake news," without banning them. As of this update no further outlet has been banned.

take: The government’s case came down to one request: that a trial judge treat two appeals-court decisions as wrongly decided. A district judge cannot do that, as this one said at the hearing and again in his order, so the argument was addressed to a higher court from its first page.

What the six days exposed matters more than the ruling. The stated reason moved from fake news, to national security, to decorum, each arriving after the one before it had been tried. When the cited stories were checked, the list included the government’s own preliminary finding, the words of its own official at a public meeting, and a background call the White House set up itself.

A press office that cannot name the rule a reporter broke has not enforced a rule. It has chosen who is allowed in the room, which is the thing the First Amendment exists to prevent. It is worth noticing who signed the brief saying so: Fox News.

corrections.text: The tracker entry this page draws on originally said the phrase "ban on the free press" appeared in no transcript of Trump's remarks. The Roll Call Factbase transcript of the September 18 Oval Office session shows him saying it. The entry also quoted him as saying "It's a very simple ban"; the transcript reads "Uh, a very simple ban." And it said Betsy Klein had covered the White House since the Obama administration; the complaint says since 2018.

An earlier version of the tracker entry this page draws on described Karem v. Trump as a 2019 decision. It is the D.C. Circuit’s 2020 opinion; the 2019 ruling in that case was the district court’s. The same entry said reporters were turned away on September 24 "in defiance" of the order. The record supports "despite": the White House filed a sworn timeline and the judge accepted it.

Later the same day, before this page was published, three quotations in the tracker entry were checked against their original sources and fixed. The restraining order's line on Sherrill and Karem had been quoted as one passage, although a citation to the government's brief sits between its two sentences; the two are now quoted separately. Trump's answer about his oath carried an "and" that the Roll Call Factbase transcript does not contain. Ari Fleischer's post had been quoted from a first sentence we could verify only as read aloud on ABC; it is now quoted from "Banning them" onward, as Newsweek published it. None of the corrections changes the meaning.
